title: Salary transparency is coming. India is still whispering the number.
description: Global pay-transparency rules are making salary ranges harder to hide, but an Indian range still needs a careful reading of fixed pay, variable pay, level, and location.
body:
Global pay-transparency rules are making salary ranges harder to hide, but an Indian range still needs a careful reading of fixed pay, variable pay, level, and location.

The global number is getting harder to hide

A candidate opens a job advert in Bengaluru and finds the usual ingredients: mission, snacks, an inspirational photograph of people laughing near a whiteboard, and no salary. The same candidate later sees a European version of the role with an actual range. Suddenly the missing number has become the loudest line in the Indian advert. The OECD’s 2026 review says pay-gap reporting is expected to become much more common by the end of 2026, with the EU Pay Transparency Directive pushing employers towards clearer job evaluation, reporting, and pre-employment information. That does not mean every Indian vacancy is about to print a range. It does mean global employers are being asked to explain how jobs are valued, and those explanations travel across hiring systems. A range is not automatically honest. A company can publish ₹12–30 lakh and still make the bottom half impossible to reach, or quietly attach a variable component that turns the upper number into decorative confetti. Transparency can expose a bargain without improving it. When you see a range, ask what it covers: fixed pay, variable pay, equity, joining payment, location allowance, or all of the above. Then ask where your experience would place you and what evidence would move you through the band. The OECD describes policy direction across countries, not the compensation of one Indian role. Treat the global shift as context. The offer letter, payroll structure, and manager conversation remain the evidence for your decision. The useful move is to treat the story as a prompt, not a verdict. Write down the evidence you can observe, the assumption you are making, and the one person or document that could settle the difference. A career decision becomes less theatrical when it has a next check.

Source context: OECD (2026) — global pay-transparency tools, reporting, and job-evaluation context

Europe is publishing the awkward range

The salary range arrives in a job post and ruins a perfectly good guessing game. Recruiters can no longer ask applicants to reveal their current pay before revealing what the role pays. Somewhere, a spreadsheet has lost its favourite column: candidate anxiety. The European change is important because it attacks an old information imbalance. Employers usually know the budget, the level, and the internal comparison. Candidates often know only the title and the hope that the number will be reasonable. Requiring a range does not end negotiation, but it moves the first conversation closer to the work being priced. Employers have a fair objection: a single range can flatten different skills, locations, and responsibilities. A small company may genuinely be learning how to price a new role. The answer is not to pretend every job has one perfect number. It is to explain the level, scope, and conditions that make the range move. Read the range as a map of the employer’s uncertainty. Ask what distinguishes the lower, middle, and upper points. If the answer is only “culture fit” or “overall impression,” ask which observable outcomes define the difference. A published range may be influenced by local implementation rules, company policy, or a role being advertised across several countries. Verify the employing entity and currency before using it as a direct comparison. That is the small discipline behind a large career choice: keep the joke, lose the certainty. Notice what is actually happening in your role, then ask whether the bargain still works for your money, learning, health, and future options.

Source context: Euronews / Indeed (2026) — how published salary information can still vary by country, role, and implementation

India hears the global echo

In India, the salary conversation often begins after three rounds of interviews and one request for the last payslip. The candidate has already invested time, disclosed a number, and watched the employer build a budget around the old number instead of the new work. Pay transparency changes the order of the conversation. It asks the employer to describe the value of the role before asking the candidate to defend their history. For Indian professionals moving from services to product, from a smaller city to a metro, or from one function to another, that distinction matters because past pay can reflect a previous bargaining position rather than current capability. A current salary can still be useful evidence in some contexts. It may reveal level, fixed-versus-variable mix, or the size of a move. The problem is treating it as an objective measure of worth. A person can be underpaid and still be asked to prove they deserve a fairer number. If asked for current compensation, separate fixed cash, variable pay, benefits, and one-time payments. Then redirect politely: “I can share the structure, but I’d like to understand the range and scope for this role.” Notice whether the conversation becomes clearer or more evasive. Disclosure practices vary by employer and role. This article is not a legal instruction to refuse a question. It is a reminder to understand what information you are exchanging and what it will be used to anchor. A headline can be true and still be a poor instruction. It may describe a pattern across the market while saying very little about your manager, contract, city, or household. Use it to form a better question, then go looking for the local answer.

Salary history is a fossil, not a forecast

A recruiter sees a previous package of ₹10 lakh and offers ₹12 lakh for a role that has a much wider mandate. The candidate is told it is a 20% hike, as if the old number were a scientific baseline preserved in amber. Salary history is a record of a past bargain. It can be shaped by city, employer brand, joining urgency, negotiation confidence, family constraints, a career break, or a function that was priced badly. None of those facts automatically describes the value of the next role. Using history as the only anchor rewards previous information gaps. Companies need a budget discipline and cannot pay every applicant whatever they request. A range is not a licence for unlimited negotiation. The fairer question is whether the company can explain the band and assess the candidate against the work rather than against a personal financial history. Build your own evidence pack: comparable responsibilities, scarce skills, measurable outcomes, location and schedule costs, and the minimum fixed cash that makes the move workable. Use it to ask for the role’s band, not to invent a market median from a single internet post. Public salary data is noisy and often mixes levels. A number from a forum, friend, or recruiter is a clue, not proof that your role should pay the same. Keep the comparison specific to scope and employer. The reader does not need another prophecy. They need a way to tell a useful signal from a polished story. Put the claim beside the cost, the evidence beside the uncertainty, and the next move beside the part that remains unknown.

A range can still be theatre

An advert says ₹15–28 lakh. The candidate imagines the middle. During the offer call, the recruiter explains that ₹15 lakh is fixed, ₹28 lakh includes an impossible target bonus, and the role is “senior” only when the workload is being described. Transparency is not the same as clarity. A range can hide conditional compensation, probation changes, joining bonuses, equity, or a location allowance that disappears after the first year. The number needs a grammar: what is certain, what is conditional, when it pays, and who controls the condition. Not every incentive is a trick. Variable pay can reward real outcomes, and a business may not know the final scope until the person joins. A candidate who demands that every component be fixed may be asking for a different job design, not merely a fairer offer. Translate the range into three columns: bankable in an ordinary month, payable if a stated target is met, and dependent on discretion or an event. Compare the role using the first column. Treat the others as upside or risk, not as rent money. Bonus plans and equity documents can be complex. If a payment is large enough to change your decision, read the actual plan or get qualified advice rather than relying on a recruiter’s cheerful summary. The useful move is to treat the story as a prompt, not a verdict. Write down the evidence you can observe, the assumption you are making, and the one person or document that could settle the difference. A career decision becomes less theatrical when it has a next check.

Negotiating after the number appears

A candidate sees a range and assumes negotiation is over. It is not. The range is an opening to ask better questions, but it is not a vending machine that dispenses the top end when someone says “I have eight years of experience” with sufficient feeling. The strongest negotiation connects evidence to the employer’s own language. If the role asks for ownership across teams, show where you have made decisions across teams. If the upper band expects customer or revenue impact, show that impact. Transparency improves the conversation only when the candidate can translate experience into the priced scope. Some candidates have strong evidence but little bargaining power because they need the job quickly. That is not a personal failure. A range can still help them reject an unaffordable process earlier and protect time that would otherwise be spent auditioning for a number that was never available. Ask three questions: “What does someone at the top of this band already demonstrate?” “Which part of my evidence maps to that?” and “What would make the company place me higher after joining?” Get the answer in writing when the difference is material. Negotiation cannot correct a role with weak management, unclear scope, or an unstable business. A higher number is not a win if the job is priced to compensate for a problem nobody will name. That is the small discipline behind a large career choice: keep the joke, lose the certainty. Notice what is actually happening in your role, then ask whether the bargain still works for your money, learning, health, and future options.

The junior candidate sees a different market

A fresher sees a range and notices that the bottom is still far below the rent in the city where the job is based. The range is transparent, but the affordability problem has not been magically promoted to the upper end. Pay transparency can reduce wasted applications without solving entry-level scarcity. Early-career candidates may have less evidence, fewer alternatives, and more pressure to accept a title in exchange for a low fixed salary. The useful gain is not always a higher offer; sometimes it is knowing the offer before spending three weekends on assignments. An entry role can be worth accepting if it teaches a real skill, provides a credible manager, and leaves enough cash and energy to remain stable. Refusing every low number can also close a bridge into a field. The decision needs more than indignation. Compare the fixed monthly cash with rent, commute, food, family support, and the time required to do the work well. Then ask what six months of evidence you would own. If the role is affordable only through debt or unpaid overtime, call that a constraint, not a motivation problem. A starting salary does not determine a whole career, but it can affect health and mobility. Do not let a market slogan pressure you into an arrangement your actual budget cannot carry. A headline can be true and still be a poor instruction. It may describe a pattern across the market while saying very little about your manager, contract, city, or household. Use it to form a better question, then go looking for the local answer.

The range does not remove the title problem

Two companies advertise “Product Manager.” One means roadmap ownership and customer discovery. The other means writing tickets, chasing approvals, and attending meetings until the calendar achieves consciousness. Pay transparency works best when job architecture is transparent too. A salary band without a useful definition of scope can make different jobs look comparable when they are not. The title, decision rights, reporting line, team size, and success measures belong beside the number. Titles are imperfect shorthand and businesses need room to design roles differently. A small company cannot reproduce the same layers as a large one. The answer is not a universal title police force; it is enough detail for a candidate to understand what the band is buying. Ask what decisions sit inside the role, what decisions require approval, and which outcomes will be reviewed after 90 days. Then compare that scope with the band. If the title is senior but the authority is junior, negotiate the work or the number accordingly. Job scope can change after hiring. Document the initial mandate, but continue checking whether the role is actually accumulating the evidence and authority promised in the interview. The reader does not need another prophecy. They need a way to tell a useful signal from a polished story. Put the claim beside the cost, the evidence beside the uncertainty, and the next move beside the part that remains unknown.

What transparency does not solve

A company publishes a range, closes the pay-history question, and still promotes the person who is most visible to a senior leader. The salary page looks modern. The career system remains powered by vibes. Pre-employment transparency can help candidates compare opportunities, but progression and internal equity require other systems: consistent levels, calibrated reviews, documented criteria, and managers who can explain decisions. The number at entry is only one moment in a longer bargain. No organisation can eliminate judgement from promotion or hiring. Different work genuinely has different impact, and context matters. A demand for perfect objectivity can become another way to hide the decisions that need explanation. Ask how the company reviews pay after hiring, when bands are updated, and how exceptions are recorded. Look for an answer with an owner and a cadence. “We take a holistic view” is not wrong, but it is incomplete until the holistic view has visible inputs. A polished compensation framework may still be applied unevenly. Speak with a future peer if possible and compare the written system with actual examples, without asking anyone to disclose private pay. The useful move is to treat the story as a prompt, not a verdict. Write down the evidence you can observe, the assumption you are making, and the one person or document that could settle the difference. A career decision becomes less theatrical when it has a next check.

The manager inherits a spreadsheet

A manager receives a team with salaries that reflect several acquisitions, hiring booms, and one employee who negotiated brilliantly while another was too polite to ask. The new transparency expectation arrives before the spreadsheet has learned to explain itself. Managers are often asked to communicate pay decisions they did not create. A fair system needs job evaluation, budget ownership, correction mechanisms, and training for difficult conversations. Otherwise transparency can expose inequity while giving the manager only a scripted apology and a frozen budget. Budgets are real and cannot always correct every gap immediately. A company may need to phase adjustments or prioritise the largest risks. The ethical test is whether the constraint is named, the path is documented, and employees are not told that an unchangeable system is the same as a fair one. If your pay concern is internal, ask what level you are mapped to, what evidence supports the mapping, and when it can be reviewed. Ask what happens if the answer is “not now.” A date and an owner are more useful than admiration. Do not infer discrimination from one comparison without context. Pay, scope, location, performance, and history can differ. The point is to request a reviewable explanation, not to conduct a private trial in the cafeteria. That is the small discipline behind a large career choice: keep the joke, lose the certainty. Notice what is actually happening in your role, then ask whether the bargain still works for your money, learning, health, and future options.

The privacy argument deserves a seat

An employee supports transparency until a group chat starts circulating everyone’s exact salaries. Suddenly the progressive policy has acquired the emotional texture of a neighbourhood WhatsApp rumour. Pay transparency can mean ranges, criteria, reporting, or individual disclosure rights; it does not necessarily mean publishing every person’s payslip. Privacy matters because salary can reveal family choices, negotiation history, or financial vulnerability. Good systems make pay legible without turning people into public data points. Employees may need information about comparable pay to identify unfairness. A rule that protects privacy so completely that nobody can challenge a gap is just secrecy wearing a cardigan. Ask what information is shared, with whom, for what purpose, and how it is protected. For a personal concern, use a defined HR or manager channel and keep the conversation about role, level, and criteria rather than gossip about a colleague’s exact number. Employment privacy rules vary by jurisdiction and company. Do not forward confidential compensation information or assume that a transparency initiative gives permission to share another person’s data. A headline can be true and still be a poor instruction. It may describe a pattern across the market while saying very little about your manager, contract, city, or household. Use it to form a better question, then go looking for the local answer.

The Indian offer call gets more specific

The recruiter says, “We can do a good hike.” The candidate replies, “What is the fixed monthly amount, what is conditional, and which level does this role sit at?” The room does not explode. It merely becomes more interesting. Specific questions make it harder for both sides to hide behind a percentage. A 30% increase can be small if the old package had low fixed pay, or large if the new role adds relocation, office attendance, or a clawback. The role’s economics need a sentence, not a celebratory emoji. Recruiters may not control all details at the first call. Insisting on a complete package before the role is understood can make a conversation unnecessarily rigid. Ask for the earliest reliable range, then revisit once scope is clear. Keep a short script: “What is the fixed range for this level?” “What variable or one-time components sit outside it?” “What location and attendance assumptions are priced into it?” “When can we confirm the complete structure?” A conversation is not a contract. Preserve the written offer and compare it with what was said. If the two differ, ask for clarification before resigning from the current role. The reader does not need another prophecy. They need a way to tell a useful signal from a polished story. Put the claim beside the cost, the evidence beside the uncertainty, and the next move beside the part that remains unknown.

A wider band can hide a wider risk

A startup offers a salary range that looks generous because the top end includes a job that may grow into three jobs. The recruiter calls it upside. The candidate calls it a future tense with a calendar invite. Wide bands can reflect genuine uncertainty about scope, level, or business need. They can also shift the risk of an evolving role onto the candidate. The higher number should come with higher clarity about authority, resources, and the evidence used to review the role. A growing company may not know exactly how the position will develop. Some candidates prefer that ambiguity because it offers access and learning they cannot get in a larger organisation. Flexibility is not automatically a defect. Ask what must be true for the role to reach the upper end: headcount, revenue, product launch, skill depth, or a promotion. Then ask what happens if that condition is delayed. Price the downside without killing the upside. No interview can forecast a startup’s next year. Treat equity, title growth, and future salary movement as possibilities unless the current cash and scope work without them. The useful move is to treat the story as a prompt, not a verdict. Write down the evidence you can observe, the assumption you are making, and the one person or document that could settle the difference. A career decision becomes less theatrical when it has a next check.

The practical transparency checklist

Before replying to an offer, a candidate writes six lines on a sticky note: fixed pay, variable pay, one-time money, level, location, and review path. The note is less glamorous than a salary calculator and more likely to prevent a bad surprise. A useful transparency check connects the number to the life it is meant to fund. It also reveals where the employer’s explanation stops. A clear range with unclear conditions is not useless, but it needs a discount in your decision. Not every unknown is a red flag. Early conversations are incomplete, and some details depend on approvals. The question is whether the missing answer is expected to arrive before commitment and whether the company treats the question as reasonable. Ask for the compensation breakup, the role level, the review cycle, and the conditions attached to every non-fixed component. Record the answer. If the total only works under the best case, decide using the ordinary case. The checklist does not replace professional advice for tax, equity, or employment law. It is a way to notice which questions deserve that advice before you sign. That is the small discipline behind a large career choice: keep the joke, lose the certainty. Notice what is actually happening in your role, then ask whether the bargain still works for your money, learning, health, and future options.

Transparency is a career signal, not a guarantee

A candidate chooses the employer that explains its band, admits where the system is still changing, and shows how progression works. The company does not promise to be perfect. It demonstrates that the number can be discussed without a ritual sacrifice. The deeper shift is cultural. A transparent employer treats compensation as part of the work design rather than a private trick played at the end of recruitment. That can make it easier to compare roles, negotiate responsibly, and notice when a title has been inflated to save money. A transparent advert can come from a difficult workplace, while a quiet employer can offer a strong manager and fair treatment. Do not turn one public signal into a complete culture score. Use transparency as one input beside manager quality, scope, stability, location, and learning. Ask whether the employer’s explanation gets more specific as the process advances. Clarity that disappears at offer stage was only marketing. Global policy movement does not settle Indian compensation practice overnight. The useful response is neither panic nor celebration. Keep asking what is fixed, what is conditional, and what the role is actually worth to your life. A headline can be true and still be a poor instruction. It may describe a pattern across the market while saying very little about your manager, contract, city, or household. Use it to form a better question, then go looking for the local answer.
